evals.prompt: Provide a complete AWS Data Perimeter design covering the three Data Perimeter invariants (Trusted Identities, Trusted Resources, Expected Networks) and write the production JSON blueprints for: (1) a Resource Control Policy (RCP) enforcing trusted Organization identities on S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager, and STS, and (2) a Service Control Policy (SCP) preventing accounts from leaving the Organization, disabling security logging, or operating outside `ap-south-1` and `us-east-1` while exempting global services.
evals.expected_output: Maps the 3 AWS Data Perimeter invariants to their policy types and condition keys (`aws:PrincipalOrgID` + `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService == false` in RCPs, `aws:ResourceOrgID` in SCPs/VPC Endpoint policies, and `aws:SourceVpc` / `aws:VpceOrgID` + `aws:ViaAWSService == true` in SCPs+RCPs), provides the `EnforceOrgIdentitiesDataPerimeter` RCP JSON (`s3:*`, `sqs:*`, `kms:*`, `secretsmanager:*`, `sts:AssumeRole` with `StringNotEqualsIfExists` on `aws:PrincipalOrgID` and `BoolIfExists` on `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService: false`), and provides the SCP JSON (`DenyLeavingOrgAndDisablingAudit` + `DenyNonApprovedRegionsExceptGlobalServices` with `NotAction` exemptions for `iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sts:*`, `route53:*`, `cloudfront:*`, `wafv2:*`, `shield:*`, `support:*`, `ce:*`, `budgets:*`, `pricing:*` and `aws:ViaAWSService: false`).
expectations: Details all three AWS Data Perimeter invariants and their condition keys: Trusted Identities (`aws:PrincipalOrgID` with `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService`), Trusted Resources (`aws:ResourceOrgID`), and Expected Networks (`aws:SourceVpc` / `aws:VpceOrgID` with `aws:ViaAWSService`)

Provides the production Resource Control Policy (RCP) JSON (`EnforceOrgIdentitiesDataPerimeter`) denying `s3:*`, `sqs:*`, `kms:*`, `secretsmanager:*`, and `sts:AssumeRole` when `aws:PrincipalOrgID` does not match and `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is `false`

Provides the SCP statement `DenyLeavingOrgAndDisablingAudit` blocking `organizations:LeaveOrganization`, `cloudtrail:StopLogging`, `cloudtrail:DeleteTrail`, `guardduty:DeleteDetector`, `securityhub:DisableSecurityHub`, `config:StopConfigurationRecorder`, and `s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock`

Provides the SCP statement `DenyNonApprovedRegionsExceptGlobalServices` using `NotAction` for global services (`iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sts:*`, `route53:*`, `cloudfront:*`, `wafv2:*`, `shield:*`, `support:*`, `ce:*`, `budgets:*`, `pricing:*`) with `aws:RequestedRegion` and `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:ViaAWSService": "false"}`

evals.prompt: Using read-only MCP calls, inspect our current AWS account identity and organization status (`sts get-caller-identity`, `organizations describe-organization`). Then design a canonical multi-account AWS Control Tower Landing Zone OU hierarchy and explain how all four AWS Organizations governance policy types (SCPs, RCPs, Declarative Policies, and Tag/Backup Policies) layer together without overlapping responsibilities.
evals.expected_output: Executes read-only MCP discovery (`sts get-caller-identity`, `organizations describe-organization`), designs the canonical AWS Organizations OU hierarchy (`Security OU` with `Log Archive` S3 Object Lock account and `Security Tooling` delegated admin account; `Infrastructure OU` with `Network Hub` and `Central DNS` accounts; `Workloads OU` with `Prod` and `NonProd` OUs; `Shared Services / Platform OU`; `Sandbox & Decommissioned OUs`), and clearly differentiates SCPs (IAM principal boundary), RCPs (resource boundary for Data Perimeter), Declarative Policies (service-level baseline enforcement like IMDSv2/EBS encryption/VPC Block Public Access that even root cannot bypass), and Tag/Backup Policies.
expectations: Executes read-only AWS discovery via MCP (such as `sts get-caller-identity` or `organizations describe-organization`) without running mutating calls

Designs the multi-account AWS Organizations OU hierarchy separating `Security OU` (`Log Archive` with immutable CloudTrail / S3 Object Lock and `Security Tooling` delegated admin for GuardDuty/Security Hub/Macie/Access Analyzer), `Infrastructure OU` (`Network Hub` and `Central DNS`), `Workloads OU` (`Prod` and `NonProd`), `Shared Services / Platform OU`, and `Sandbox & Decommissioned OUs`

Clearly distinguishes Service Control Policies (SCPs — restricting maximum permissions of IAM principals) from Resource Control Policies (RCPs — restricting maximum permissions on AWS resources like `s3`, `sts`, `kms`, `sqs`, `secretsmanager` for the Data Perimeter)

Explains Declarative Policies (enforcing service-level baseline state such as EC2 IMDSv2 `HttpTokens: required`, EBS encryption by default, AMI Block Public Sharing, and VPC Block Public Access, which cannot be bypassed even by account root) alongside Tag Policies and Backup Policies

evals.prompt: /aws-networking:design-hub-spoke Inspect our current ap-south-1 networking resources via read-only MCP calls and query awspricing for networking costs. Then evaluate and recommend the optimal AWS networking topology across four enterprise scenarios: (1) a global backbone across 4 Regions with 60+ VPCs and SD-WAN integration, (2) a single-Region hub-and-spoke in ap-south-1 for 25 VPCs with centralized AWS Network Firewall inspection, (3) 12 high-bandwidth microservice accounts in ap-south-1 wanting to avoid `$0.02/GB` Transit Gateway data processing charges, and (4) connecting ECS, EKS, and Lambda services across acquired accounts that have overlapping `10.0.0.0/16` IPv4 CIDRs.
evals.expected_output: Executes `/aws-networking:design-hub-spoke` using read-only MCP discovery in `ap-south-1` and `awspricing` queries, and matches each scenario to its optimal pattern: (1) AWS Cloud WAN (Core Network Policy segments `Prod`, `NonProd`, `Shared` and Service Insertion for Network Firewall), (2) AWS Transit Gateway with a dedicated Inspection VPC (`ApplianceModeSupport: enable` on the inspection attachment), (3) Shared VPC via AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) (eliminating `$0.02/GB` TGW data processing fees and sharing NAT/Interface Endpoints), and (4) Amazon VPC Lattice (`ServiceNetwork` + `AuthPolicy: AWS_IAM` supporting overlapping IPv4 CIDRs with mTLS and SigV4 auth).
expectations: Executes read-only MCP discovery in `ap-south-1` and queries `awspricing` for networking cost data

Recommends AWS Cloud WAN (with declarative Core Network Policy segments and Network Function Group service insertion) for the 60+ VPC multi-Region global backbone, replacing manual inter-Region TGW peering meshes
Recommends AWS Transit Gateway with a dedicated Inspection VPC and `ApplianceModeSupport: enable` for the single-Region 25-VPC hub-and-spoke topology

Recommends Shared VPC via AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for high-bandwidth same-Region microservices across accounts to eliminate `$0.02/GB` TGW data processing fees and share NAT Gateway / Interface Endpoint hourly costs
Recommends Amazon VPC Lattice (`ServiceNetwork` with `AuthPolicy: AWS_IAM`) for L7 cross-VPC communication across overlapping `10.0.0.0/16` IPv4 CIDRs without TGW route table complexity

evals.prompt: We are designing hybrid connectivity for SAP-C02 production resilience: (1) Our architect ordered 2 Direct Connect connections at a single Equinix Mumbai colocation facility and claims this qualifies for the 99.99% Direct Connect SLA. (2) For a secondary site with 1 DX connection (`10.0.0.0/16` summary route) and a backup Site-to-Site VPN terminating on the same Transit Gateway (`10.0.1.0/24` specific route), all traffic to `10.0.1.0/24` is using the slow VPN instead of Direct Connect! Diagnose both errors and detail the exact BGP Local Preference communities, Public VIF scope communities, outbound path selection order, and DX encryption options.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the 99.99% Direct Connect SLA requires at least 2 Direct Connect Locations (diverse physical facilities) with 2 customer routers per location (4 total connections) terminating into a Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway via Transit VIF. Explains the Longest Prefix Match gotcha: TGW prefers DX over VPN only when prefix lengths are identical (`/16` vs `/16`); because VPN advertised a more specific `/24` than DX's `/16`, VPN won! Details AWS BGP Local Preference communities (`7224:7300` High, `7224:7200` Medium, `7224:7100` Low), Public VIF scope communities (`7224:9100` local Region, `7224:9200` continent, `7224:9300` global), AWS outbound path evaluation order, and encryption over DX (IEEE 802.1AE MACsec vs IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over DX with ECMP).
expectations: Corrects the SLA assumption: achieving the 99.99% Direct Connect SLA requires at least 2 physically diverse Direct Connect Locations with 2 customer routers per location (4 connections total) terminating on a Direct Connect Gateway + Transit Gateway via Transit VIF

Diagnoses the VPN routing anomaly: Transit Gateway evaluates Longest Prefix Match first, so the VPN's `/24` route beat Direct Connect's `/16` summary route; identical prefix lengths must be advertised on both DX and backup VPN so DX wins automatically

Lists the exact AWS Direct Connect BGP Local Preference communities (`7224:7100` Low, `7224:7200` Medium, `7224:7300` High) and Public VIF scope control communities (`7224:9100` local Region, `7224:9200` continent, `7224:9300` global)

States the exact AWS -> On-Premises outbound path evaluation order: (1) Longest Prefix Match, (2) BGP Local Preference Community (`7224:7300 > 7224:7200 > 7224:7100`), (3) Same-region/Home-region DX location preference, (4) Shortest `AS_PATH`, (5) Lowest `MED`

Contrasts the two Direct Connect encryption patterns: Layer-2 IEEE 802.1AE MACsec on dedicated 10G/100G/400G ports versus Layer-3 IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect with ECMP across tunnels to scale beyond 1.25 Gbps per tunnel

evals.prompt: Our cloud security team attached two new AWS Organizations policies that immediately broke production: (1) A Region-lock SCP with `"Effect": "Deny", "Action": "*", "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-south-1"]}}` broke IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, WAFv2 global, Shield, and Cost Explorer, as well as AWS services calling KMS on our behalf! (2) A Data Perimeter RCP denying `s3:*` and `kms:*` when `aws:PrincipalOrgID != o-abc123` broke AWS CloudTrail and S3 Server Access Logging delivery! Explain why both policies broke AWS and provide the corrected JSON conditions.
evals.expected_output: Explains that the Region-lock SCP failed because global services (`iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sts:*`, `route53:*`, `cloudfront:*`, `wafv2:*`, `shield:*`, `support:*`, `ce:*`, `budgets:*`, `pricing:*`) execute in `us-east-1` and must be exempted via `NotAction`, and AWS service-initiated calls require `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:ViaAWSService": "false"}`. Explains that the Data Perimeter RCP failed because AWS service principals (like CloudTrail) do not have the customer's `aws:PrincipalOrgID` and require `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"}` alongside `StringNotEqualsIfExists` on `aws:PrincipalOrgID`. Provides both corrected JSON policies.
expectations: Explains that the Region-lock SCP must use `NotAction` to exempt global services (`iam:*`, `organizations:*`, `sts:*`, `route53:*`, `cloudfront:*`, `wafv2:*`, `shield:*`, `support:*`, `ce:*`, `budgets:*`, `pricing:*`) whose control planes operate in `us-east-1`

Explains that the Region-lock SCP (and network perimeter policies) must include `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:ViaAWSService": "false"}` so downstream calls made by AWS services on the customer's behalf are not blocked

Explains that the Data Perimeter RCP must use `StringNotEqualsIfExists` on `aws:PrincipalOrgID` paired with `"BoolIfExists": {"aws:PrincipalIsAWSService": "false"}` so AWS service principals (`PrincipalIsAWSService: true`) are exempted
Provides the complete corrected SCP and RCP JSON policy documents

evals.prompt: Our company has 80 developers and runs Production, Staging, Sandbox, CloudTrail logs, and Shared Networking inside a single monolithic AWS account using IAM tag conditions for separation. Furthermore, account admins keep turning off EC2 IMDSv2 (`HttpTokens: optional`), disabling default EBS encryption, and sharing public AMIs. Why is a monolithic account an anti-pattern, how should we partition accounts in AWS Control Tower, and which specific AWS Organizations policy type prevents even an account root user from weakening IMDSv2, EBS encryption, or VPC Block Public Access?
evals.expected_output: Explains the blast radius, quota contention, and audit weaknesses of a single monolithic AWS account, presents the multi-account AWS Control Tower OU architecture (`Security OU` with `Log Archive` S3 Object Lock + `Security Tooling` delegated admin; `Infrastructure OU` with `Network Hub` + `Central DNS`; `Workloads OU` with `Prod` and `NonProd`; `Shared Services / Platform OU`; `Sandbox & Decommissioned OUs`), and identifies AWS Organizations **Declarative Policies** as the mechanism that enforces baseline service-level configuration state (EC2 IMDSv2 `HttpTokens: required`, EBS encryption by default, AMI Block Public Sharing, VPC Block Public Access) even against account root.
expectations: Explains why running Prod, NonProd, Sandbox, Security Logs, and Networking in a single monolithic AWS account is an anti-pattern (blast radius, API/service quota contention, lack of hard billing/security boundaries, mutable logs)

Prescribes the canonical AWS Control Tower OU hierarchy including a dedicated `Log Archive` account (with immutable CloudTrail and S3 Object Lock) and `Security Tooling` account (delegated admin for GuardDuty, Security Hub, Macie, Access Analyzer)

Identifies AWS Organizations **Declarative Policies** as the policy type that enforces service-level baseline configurations (`HttpTokens: required` for IMDSv2, EBS encryption by default, AMI Block Public Sharing, VPC Block Public Access) and cannot be bypassed even by the member account root user

evals.prompt: Using read-only MCP calls in ap-south-1, check our VPC Endpoints (`describe-vpc-endpoints`) and Route 53 Hosted Zones (`list-hosted-zones`), and query awspricing for VPC Endpoint pricing. Then design a Centralized PrivateLink Endpoint Hub and Hybrid DNS architecture for 25 AWS accounts so we don't pay duplicate Interface Endpoint hourly charges in every spoke account.
evals.expected_output: Runs read-only MCP discovery (`describe-vpc-endpoints`, `list-hosted-zones`) and `awspricing` queries, and designs the Centralized PrivateLink & Hybrid DNS architecture: provision Interface VPC Endpoints (`ssm`, `ssmmessages`, `sts`, `kms`, `logs`, `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, `bedrock-runtime`) in a central Endpoint VPC with `PrivateDnsEnabled: false`, create a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone (PHZ) for each service domain pointing to the central Endpoint ENIs, share those PHZs plus Route 53 Resolver Inbound/Outbound rules across spoke VPCs using Route 53 Profiles (`AWS::Route53Profiles::Profile`), and keep S3 and DynamoDB as free Gateway Endpoints inside each spoke VPC.
expectations: Executes read-only MCP discovery in `ap-south-1` (`describe-vpc-endpoints`, `list-hosted-zones`) and queries `awspricing`
Specifies provisioning Interface VPC Endpoints (`ssm`, `ssmmessages`, `sts`, `kms`, `logs`, `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, `bedrock-runtime`) in a central Endpoint VPC with `PrivateDnsEnabled: false`

Specifies creating a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone (PHZ) per service domain pointing to the central Endpoint ENIs and sharing the PHZs across spoke VPCs using Route 53 Profiles (`AWS::Route53Profiles::Profile`), saving ~$21.60/month per endpoint per spoke account
Keeps Amazon S3 and DynamoDB as free Gateway VPC Endpoints inside each individual spoke VPC rather than routing them through the central Interface Endpoint hub

Includes centralizing Route 53 Resolver Inbound Endpoints (for on-premises -> AWS DNS) and Outbound Endpoints + Forwarding Rules (for AWS -> on-premises DNS) in the Central Network/DNS Account and sharing them via Route 53 Profiles or AWS RAM

evals.prompt: In our 30-account hub-and-spoke network, an engineer: (1) provisioned paid S3 and DynamoDB Interface VPC Endpoints in all 30 spoke VPCs instead of Gateway Endpoints, and (2) in our Central Endpoint Hub VPC, created centralized Interface Endpoints for `ecr.api` and `bedrock-runtime` with `PrivateDnsEnabled: true` and then got an error trying to create custom Route 53 Private Hosted Zones for `api.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com` and `bedrock-runtime.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com` to share via Route 53 Profiles! Explain both mistakes and how to fix them.
evals.expected_output: Explains both mistakes: (1) S3 and DynamoDB should be deployed as free **Gateway VPC Endpoints** directly inside each spoke VPC to avoid hourly and per-GB PrivateLink Interface Endpoint charges (reserving centralized Interface Endpoints for services like `ssm`, `sts`, `kms`, `logs`, `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, `bedrock-runtime`), and (2) in a Centralized PrivateLink Hub, the central Interface VPC Endpoints must be created with `PrivateDnsEnabled: false` so you can create custom Route 53 Private Hosted Zones pointing to the central Endpoint ENIs and share them across spoke VPCs via Route 53 Profiles (`AWS::Route53Profiles::Profile`).
expectations: Explains that S3 and DynamoDB should use free **Gateway VPC Endpoints** inside each spoke VPC rather than paid Interface Endpoints across 30 spoke VPCs

Explains why creating the custom Private Hosted Zones failed: when `PrivateDnsEnabled: true` is set on an Interface VPC Endpoint, AWS automatically creates a managed Private Hosted Zone for that domain, which conflicts with creating and sharing a custom PHZ

Prescribes setting `PrivateDnsEnabled: false` on the central Hub VPC's Interface Endpoints (`ecr.api`, `bedrock-runtime`, `ssm`, `sts`, `kms`, `logs`), creating custom Route 53 Private Hosted Zones pointing to the central Endpoint ENIs, and associating those PHZs across spoke VPCs using **Route 53 Profiles** (`AWS::Route53Profiles::Profile`)
